original_idea.body:
# Follow-up: Why Did Performance Accelerate in H2 2025? Attribution Analysis of the Cybench Inflection

**Problem:** Cybench performance went from ~10% to 82% in 18 months with an apparent inflection point in H2 2025. The causes of this inflection are not understood. Was it model capability improvements, better scaffolding, increased token budgets, or benchmark contamination from training on CTF writeups?

**Direction:** Use publicly available model release dates, Cybench leaderboard data, and major scaffolding improvement announcements to build a timeline. Test three hypotheses: (H1) capability jump correlates with model releases, (H2) capability jump correlates with token budget increases, (H3) capability jump correlates with CTF writeup publication dates. Perform a simple regression analysis of performance on time-series variables.

**Why it matters:** If the inflection was primarily driven by contamination (H3), the 82% figure is misleading. If driven by capability (H1) or inference compute (H2), it is a genuine threat signal. Attribution analysis is critical for calibrating alarm levels and projecting future capability trajectories.

**Relevant context:** Irregular 2026 'Emerging Evidence of Capability Shift' documented Cybench 10%→82%, inflection H2 2025. AISI noted log-linear compute scaling. CAIBench meta-benchmark noted saturation concerns. CTFusion addressed reuse issues. NYU CTF Bench (ICLR 2025) published with full leaderboard data.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Retrospective analysis is valuable but has unclear direct pathway to reducing catastrophic risk.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Data analysis and visualization; students with Python skills can handle with mentorship on statistical methods.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Scope is too broad for 30 hours; requires multiple sub-experiments or extensive infrastructure setup.
